evidence.quote: The application of standards remains voluntary. Providers can choose any other framework to demonstrate their compliance with the AI Act. However, harmonised standards referenced in the Official Journal of the EU provide legal certainty. Companies that apply harmonised standards are presumed to be compliant with the legal requirements.

compliance_deadlines: Before placement on the market (high-risk AI system requirements under the AI Act)
2027-12-02 (latest proposed applicability date under the Digital Omnibus for Annex III high-risk AI systems, subject to earlier application if support tools and standards are available)

2028-08-02 (latest proposed applicability date under the Digital Omnibus for Annex I EU harmonisation legislation AI systems, subject to earlier application if support tools and standards are available)
policy_extraction.implementation_notes: Informational policy webpage published by the European Commission explaining AI Act standardisation rather than a binding legal instrument or technical standard itself. Harmonised standards developed by CEN and CENELEC (via JTC 21) across ten requested areas remain voluntary, but once assessed by the Commission and referenced in the Official Journal of the EU they provide a presumption of conformity. Notes that prEN 18286 (Quality Management System for AI Act Article 17) entered public enquiry on 30 October 2025, highlights international alignment with ISO/IEC SC 42, and summarizes the 19 November 2025 Digital Omnibus proposal linking high-risk AI rule applicability to the availability of standards and support tools.

risk_framing.rationale_summary: Innovation enablement is the dominant frame because the page justifies AI Act standardisation primarily as a way to provide legal certainty, simplify compliance, lower compliance costs for businesses of all sizes, avoid regulatory fragmentation and redundant compliance efforts, and foster trust and market acceptance through voluntary technical standards and rollout support tools. Economic competitiveness is a close runner-up, reflected in repeated emphasis on European harmonised standards becoming de facto global benchmarks, helping developers compete on a global scale, and positioning the EU to lead globally; innovation enablement edges it out because the operational focus throughout the page is reducing compliance friction and enabling trustworthy adoption rather than zero-sum economic rivalry. Consumer and public safety and fundamental rights appear as secondary background rationales describing the underlying high-risk AI Act objectives (protecting safety, health, and fundamental rights, and meeting high safety standards).
